spec_choices.why: The designer chose 3, and an auction needs at least two rivals for ties and bid-reading to matter. Above 5, the talk and announcements grow long and each player wins too few of the 6 auctions for budgeting to matter.

The rules require it, and players genuinely disagree: everyone wants rivals to back off. Bluffs and threats about which auctions they value give players something to reason about, and since talk is not binding, believing it can be costly.

spec_choices.what: prize_points visible only to its owner
spec_choices.why: The rules announce only the winner and coins. Publishing prize_points would reveal the winner's private value for that auction.
The rules say entry k is the value for auction k, and auction runs from 1 to 6.

This is an all-pay auction, so overbidding is costly and ties waste both bids. A thoughtful player rations 100 coins over 6 auctions, pushes on high-value auctions, watches rivals' committed totals between stages, and avoids matching a rival's total.

simplifications.why: This keeps the flat step list clear without a scratch stage counter, and the behaviour is identical.

variation.original_summary: The dollar auction: two players take turns raising an open bid for a $1 bill by at least $0.05. When one drops out, the high bidder pays their bid and takes the dollar, and the runner-up pays their bid and gets nothing, so sunk costs push bids past the prize's value.

review.evidence: With two players and 'higher total wins', only the difference matters. Opening at $0.05 and dropping out at once wins or draws against a bidder who also drops. Once escalation starts, the player willing to go further always wins the difference, so the game becomes a pure war of attrition where never yielding cannot lose. The first bidder also holds a built-in turn-order position.
There is no luck, but nothing to out-think either: the prize is common and known, and both players see every bid. The outcome depends on stubbornness, not insight.
One auction for one known prize. The analysis ends with 'bid once or escalate forever', and there is no repeated structure to learn from.
It is a perfect-information game: the prize value, every bid and the high bidder are all public. Nothing is hidden to infer.
Payoffs are pure arithmetic on bids: 1 - bid for the winner and -bid for the others.
It is text-only and arithmetic. However, alternating raises with no cap can run for an unbounded number of turns, and dropping out is a sequential sub-loop of variable length.

problems: P1: Two-player 'higher total wins' reduces the game to a war of attrition in which refusing to yield, or never bidding, cannot lose.
P2: Perfect information. The prize value and all bids are public, so there is nothing to infer about opponents.
P3: A single auction gives no multi-round planning and no budget trade-offs.
P4: Alternating unbounded raises cannot be built as a fixed flat step list, and they give the first bidder a positional edge.

P5 (previous build): the raise poll's option range read a scratch attribute (raise/stage_raise) that stayed 0. Every seat was offered only 0, committed never grew, and coins never fell (tests R5 to R8 failed).
P6 (previous build): too many redundant parameter attributes (prize_value_1..6, prize_value_total) alongside scratch attributes, which wasted the attribute budget and invited wrong references.

changes.what: Three to five players, with the winner decided by the highest final score (coins left plus prize points).
changes.why: One rival's gain is not every other's loss, and a player who sits out every auction is overtaken by anyone who wins a prize cheaply.

changes.what: Each player privately holds a value list: a random order of [10, 15, 20, 25, 30, 40], one value per auction. Only the owner sees it.
changes.why: Each player must infer from bids and talk who values the current prize highly. Every list has the same total of 140, so the deal changes what to do, not who is ahead.

changes.what: Six auctions drawn from one budget of 100 coins.
changes.why: Players must plan when to spend: whether to chase their 40-auction or win cheap prizes others ignore. They can also read opponents' remaining budgets.

changes.what: Each auction has exactly three simultaneous sealed raise stages. Committed bids are announced after each stage, and it is all-pay: everyone pays their committed total.
changes.why: This keeps the dollar auction's sunk-cost escalation in a fixed, buildable number of steps with no seat order.

changes.what: Ties at the top bid produce no winner, though everyone still pays.
changes.why: Matching an opponent is not safe, so the 'can't lose' option disappears.

changes.what: The raise poll's options are every whole number from 0 to (that player's coins − that player's committed), read live from those two player attributes at that moment. The chosen raise is added straight to committed. There are no scratch raise/stage_raise attributes.
changes.why: This removes the source of the 0-only option range, so bids accumulate and coins are deducted at resolution.

changes.what: Only the parameters actually used are kept as attributes (starting_coins, auctions, raise_stages, min_winning_bid, prize_deck). prize_value_1..6 and prize_value_total are dropped.
changes.why: This keeps the attribute count small and stops references to stale values.

changes.what: A simultaneous one-message talk phase before the first raise stage of each auction.
changes.why: Only one player can win each auction, so players disagree. They can bluff a high value to scare others off or feign disinterest, and listeners must judge it against bidding behaviour.

keeps: Bidding for a prize where losing bidders still pay their bids (all-pay).
Escalation through repeated raises on top of what you have already committed, with sunk-cost pressure.
Public committed bids after each raise, so players see the war of attrition unfold.
Highest bidder takes the prize, and the net gain is prize minus bid.

recommendation.reason: The sunk-cost escalation is worth keeping. Private values, a shared multi-auction budget, more players and fixed sealed raise stages turn it into an inference-and-budgeting game within the limits.

variation.name: Escalation Auction
variation.summary: Three to five players with 100 coins each bid in six all-pay auctions. Each auction has three sealed raise stages, and committed bids are revealed after each stage. Each player privately values each prize differently, so they must read rivals' values from talk and bids and spend their budget wisely.
variation.rules:
PARAMETERS (stored as table attributes): starting_coins = 100; auctions = 6; raise_stages = 3; min_winning_bid = 1; prize_deck = [10, 15, 20, 25, 30, 40].

R1 Setup: every player has coins = 100, prize_points = 0, committed = 0, final_score = 0. Table: auction = 0, top_bid = 0, top_count = 0, auction_winner = 'none'.

R2 Private values: at setup each player is dealt their own values list, a random order of [10, 15, 20, 25, 30, 40] (total 140), visible only to its owner. Entry k is that player's value for auction k. Players' lists are dealt independently, so two players may hold the same value for the same auction.

Each round is one auction. There are 6 rounds.

R3 Round start: auction increases by 1 and every player's committed is set to 0. Each player is privately told their value for this auction (entry number 'auction' of their values list). Everyone is told the auction number and every player's current coins.

R4 Talk: every player writes one short message at the same time, without seeing the others. All messages are then shown to everyone. Messages are not binding and change no numbers.

R5 Raise stage (runs 3 times per auction): all players choose at the same time a raise, a whole number from 0 up to (their own coins − their own committed). The range is computed for each player at that moment from their current coins and committed attributes. For example, it is 0..100 at the start of an auction with 100 coins, and 0..55 for a player with 85 coins who committed 30 earlier in the same auction. Immediately after the poll, each player's committed increases by the raise they chose.

R6 Budget limit: a player can never commit more than their coins in one auction. With coins 40 and committed 30, the options are exactly 0 to 10.

R7 Announcement: after each of the 3 raise stages, every player's committed total is announced to all.

R8 Resolution, payment: after the third stage, top_bid = the highest committed, and top_count = the number of players whose committed equals top_bid. Every player's coins decrease by their committed, whether or not they won. For example, bids of 20, 15 and 0 leave coins of 80, 85 and 100 from 100 each.

R9 Resolution, prize: if top_count = 1 and top_bid ≥ 1, that player is the auction_winner and adds their own value for this auction to prize_points. Otherwise auction_winner = 'none' and nobody gets a prize. The winner and every player's coins are announced. Each player's committed is then reset to 0.

R10 End: after the 6th auction, each player's final_score = coins + prize_points.
variation.objective: After 6 auctions, the player with the highest final_score (coins remaining + prize_points) wins. If several players tie for the highest final_score, the game is a draw among them.
variation.expected_effect: Players disagree on every auction: only one can take the prize, and each values it differently in secret. Talk becomes bluffing ('this one is my 40, back off') and probing. A player who just believes a claim and drops out can lose a cheap prize to a bluffer, and one who escalates to call a bluff can pour coins into a prize worth little to them, because losers pay too. Always bidding 0 loses to anyone who wins one prize for a few coins. Bidding everything early wastes the budget, since prizes are worth at most 40 but cost the bid either way. Matching a rival risks a tie in which both pay and neither wins. Good play means inferring rivals' values from their escalation patterns and remaining coins, conceding contested auctions, and sniping uncontested ones. Value lists have equal totals and there is no seat order, so the deal changes what to do, not who is ahead.

balanced.evidence: Main decision: in each auction you pay all of your committed coins whether you win or not (all-pay), and you score your private value v (10-40) only if your bid is the single highest. Net per auction: a sole top bidder gets v - b; everyone else gets -b. A player who bids 0 loses 0. Example with 3 players, v = 25 for player A. Bids (1,0,0): A +24, the others 0. Bids (10,9,0): A +15, B -9, C 0. Bids (20,20,0): a tie, so no prize; A -20, B -20, C 0. Thoughtless policies under the winner rule (highest coins + prize_points): (1) Always 0 (always pass) ends on exactly 100. Against random opponents it wins, because random bidders burn coins. Against sensible play it loses whenever any opponent wins even one auction for less than its value; one auction won for 1 coin on a 10-value already gives 109 > 100. Over 6 auctions a sensible player bids low in auctions where the others are quiet. In contested auctions, standard all-pay results give roughly zero expected surplus with large variance. The best of 2-4 opponents therefore usually ends above 100, so pass does not win or draw almost every time. (2) Always the last (highest) option: commit all 100 coins in stage 1 of auction 1. This ends on at most 40 (or 0 on a tie) and loses to everyone, including a passer. (3) Always the highest bid in general, matching the top bid: ties void the prize and both players pay, so it bleeds coins. (4) Random play: uniform 0..remaining in stage 1 spends about 50 coins in auction 1 alone, so it loses to both the passer and sensible play. No option is strictly better whatever others do. Bidding 0 is beaten by bidding just above the others when they bid low. Bidding high is beaten by bidding 0 when others bid high. Seats are symmetric: all choices are simultaneous polls and all players get the same public information. Every player's value multiset is the same (total 140), so the deal gives no systematic edge. Any player can win. The examples check out: 85 coins with 30 committed gives 0..55; bids 20/15/0 from 100 give 80/85/100.

playable.evidence: Rules are complete. Setup, value deal, the 3 simultaneous raise stages with a range computed from coins - committed, announcements, payment, prize (sole top with top_bid >= 1, otherwise none) and the end score are all specified. Edge cases are covered: all bids 0 gives no winner; a tie at the top gives no prize but everyone pays. Coins cannot go negative (R6). The game is finite (6 auctions) and decided by arithmetic on kept attributes. Limits are met: 18 steps (<=20); 4 choice steps (talk + 3 raises, <=4); 15 attributes (<=20); 1 hidden element (the values list, <=3); 0 random draws per round (the shuffle is at setup); 6 rounds (<=40). It uses only supported features: private_values, simultaneous_choice, numeric_bids, free_text_talk, fixed_rounds. No board, judge or clock is needed. Talk with 3-5 players is justified because players disagree about who should take each auction. A proposal such as 'I take this one, you take the next' is costly to follow and can be betrayed, which gives something to reason about. Talk is simultaneous. There is no cooperate/defect late-round collapse: in the final auction, bidding below your value still pays, so late rounds stay live. The prize_deck parameter is only the source of the value list. That is cosmetic, not ambiguous.

reasoning_over_luck.evidence: Every player holds the same six values in a different order, so total potential value is identical (140) for all. Chance only affects how often high values collide in the same auction, which I estimate at about 20-30% of outcome variance. The rest is opponent modelling and planning. There is a lot to infer and act on: (a) others' private values, read from talk and from the stage 1-2 committed totals; (b) others' remaining coins, which are public and cap their bids; (c) where to concentrate a limited budget across 6 auctions, since saving coins for your 40-value auction matters; (d) the blind final stage, where you must predict last-moment raises and avoid voiding ties. Suppose all players play well: concede auctions where others have revealed high values, contest only where your value is high, and keep bids low through signalling. Then results depend on reading and exploiting rivals' bluffs and budgets, not on the deal alone. A careless bidder bleeds coins in all-pay contests and is clearly beaten by a careful one.

In the game, no seat was ever offered 5, 10, 20 or even 100, so every raise came out 0 and coins never dropped. The raise-choice options in the game file are wrong. This is not a rules or platform problem.
triage.guidance: Fix the three simultaneous raise stages so each player's options are the whole-number range 0 .. (you.coins - you.committed). With 100 coins and 0 committed the range is 0..100. With 40 coins and 30 committed it is 0..10. Build the range from those attributes, not from a fixed or empty list or from stage_raise. After each stage, add the chosen raise to `committed`. At resolution, subtract each player's `committed` from their `coins` whether or not they won. Then award the prize to the unique top bidder only if their bid is at least min_winning_bid: add their own value for the current auction to prize_points and set auction_winner. Reset `committed` to 0 after the auction. Also check that the stage choice is actually the move the players make: in the trace, all 9 recorded moves were 0 and the scripted options never matched. Keep the talk step as a simultaneous free-text poll before stage 1.

Use a numeric range with that expression as its maximum, not a stale scratch attribute such as `raise` or `stage_raise`, which stays at 0. It must offer every whole number from 0 up to `coins - committed`, worked out for each player at that moment: 0..100 at the start of an auction, 0..10 when coins are 40 and committed is 30. Make the range bound read the live player attributes and not a scratch value that is still 0 (your `raise` or `stage_raise` look like the culprit). Set `auction_winner` only when exactly one player holds the top bid and it is at least `min_winning_bid`; that player adds their own value for this auction to `prize_points`. triage.reason: The rules use a per-player numeric bid range, which the platform supports through numeric_bids. In every failing scenario the raise poll put no option above 0 to any seat (5, 40 and 100 were never offered, and all moves were 0), so the bug is in the game file's raise step, not in the tests or the rules.
triage.guidance:
Fix the raise poll in R5.
- Make each of the 3 raise stages one simultaneous numeric choice for every player.
- Set the minimum to the `min_raise` attribute (0).
- Set the maximum to `you.coins - you.committed`, evaluated per player at the moment of the poll. It must not be a fixed 0, a value from a scratch attribute that was never set (such as `stage_raise`), or a computation that comes out to 0.
- The choice must offer every whole number from 0 up to that maximum: 0..100 at 100 coins and 0 committed, 0..55 at 85 coins and 30 committed, 0..10 at 40 coins and 30 committed.
- Right after each poll, add the chosen raise to that player's `committed`, then announce everyone's `committed`.

After the third stage:
- Set `top_bid` to the maximum `committed`.
- Set `top_count` to the number of players whose `committed` equals `top_bid`.
- Subtract each player's `committed` from their `coins`, whether or not they won.
- If `top_count` = `winning_top_count` and `top_bid` >= `min_winning_bid`, set `auction_winner` to that seat and add their `current_value` to their `prize_points`.
- Only then reset `committed` to 0. Do not reset it before `top_bid` and the payment are computed.

Use the parameter attributes rather than literal numbers in the steps.
